englishChanges.before: Now here in Athens, and in Lacedaemon, the rules about love are perplexing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to grasp. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries that have no gift for eloquence, the rules are very straightforward — the law is simply in favor of these connections, and no one, young or old, says a word against them. The reason, I suppose, is that the men there are not eloquent, so lovers prefer not to take the trouble of pleading their case. In Ionia, on the other hand, and in other places generally subject to the barbarians, the custom is held to be dishonorable. There, love between males shares the evil reputation attached to philosophy and gymnastics, because all three are hostile to tyranny. Rulers' interests require that their subjects be poor in spirit and that no strong bond of friendship or fellowship form among them — and love, more than any other motive, is likely to inspire such bonds, as our own Athenian tyrants learned by experience. For Aristogeiton's love and Harmodius's constancy proved strong enough to bring down their power.
